title: The last coal orders stop at Muileann chrom
summary: The Board's clerk at Muileann chrom stops writing coal orders for the shorter hauls, An Sloc Mòr running three days in the week where it ran six. The coal engines are worked on the shorter runs alone through the summer while the dubhan engine takes the long haul to Cathair dhearg.

title: The Board's notice on the shed door
summary: A notice at Muileann chrom stands the coal engines down pending the Board's further order and calls the men who drove and fired them for instruction on the new engines, at the driver's rate while they learn. It says nothing of a man who does not learn, nor of what is to be done with the engines standing idle.

title: The Frisealach brothers put their names down
summary: Somhairle and Uilleam Frisealach, young firemen of the yard rows at Muileann chrom, ask Eachann mac Ruairidh what the new engine is like to drive and put their names down together for instruction. Their father, near the end of his own driving, says nothing and puts down none.

title: Dòmhnall Ruadh gives up the new engine
summary: Dòmhnall Ruadh, a driver of thirty years on Slighe a' Ghuail, cannot learn to read the dubhan engine's valve as he read a coal engine's fire, and after nine days strikes his name from the Board's instruction list. He asks to be kept on at the sidings or the stores instead.

title: The nine coal engines stand in the long siding
summary: By the feast of Samhain the last of the nine coal engines of Muileann chrom stands cold in the long siding with its fire drawn, and no order comes to light any of them again. The Board sends a clerk once, in spring, to count and write down their condition, and touches them with no order after.

title: An Taigh-seinnse Reòta keeps its rooms unlit
summary: Murchadh Frisealach, landlord of An Taigh-seinnse Reòta on the north road, writes to the Board that the reek of dubhan will drive custom from his house as it has from three houses on the coast. The letter is repeated at firesides between Muileann fhada and the capital as proof a house may hold to the old ways.

title: The Reòta puts in the new lamps
summary: Within the year the dubhan bus between Caol mhòr and the capital brings the Reòta more trade in a month than the old coaching road brought it in a season, and guests who stop there complain of the reek of tallow. Murchadh Frisealach lights the taproom and his two best rooms with dubhan, and keeps one wick lamp over the stable door out of what he calls habit.

title: The Board's surveyor writes Muileann dhearg spent
summary: A surveyor of the Mine Board walks the last working face at Muileann dhearg with the pit captain Gilleasbaig Ruadh and two of the older hewers, and writes in his book that the seam is spent below the value of working it. The pit is ordered to close at the month's end.

title: The last shift comes up at Muileann dhearg
summary: Twelve hewers come up the shaft at Muileann dhearg on its last morning, having spent their final two days drawing props and rails for scrap rather than cutting coal. Aonghas Dubh, last out, carries the shift's last lamp and finds no one waiting to take it; the pit captain hangs it unlit on the rack himself.

title: The guild finds carts for the walk to Seann Toll
summary: Tormod mac Dhonnchaidh, master of the Guild of Hewers, goes door to door through the pit quarter of Muileann dhearg after the closing to promise carts for what the forty remaining households cannot carry, the Board having offered places at Seann Toll but no removal. He walks the ten miles of river road with them himself.

title: The Hewers' Row named at Seann Toll
summary: The Rail Board's new row of houses on the flooding ground at the edge of Seann Toll takes the families of Muileann dhearg. The town calls it the Hewers' Row before the last house is roofed, and the name holds in the Board's own letters within the year.

title: Few of Muileann dhearg take to the river
summary: The close river trade of Seann Toll's own boatmen takes on only two or three of the young men of the Hewers' Row that winter. Most of the households go instead to the dubhan tanks at the landing, rolling barrels and minding pumps for a trade none of them was born to.

title: Tormod mac Dhonnchaidh speaks of the lamp
summary: Walking the frozen street of the Hewers' Row with Gilleasbaig Ruadh, Tormod mac Dhonnchaidh says it was not the pit's closing that undid him at Muileann dhearg but the sight of a lamp with no one left to hand it to, and names the landlord of An Taigh-seinnse Reòta a man doing the same in his own house.

title: The druid house of Muileann dhearg given to its caretaker
summary: The druid house above the emptied pit quarter of Muileann dhearg passes to Padraig Iarna, who has swept its floor and rung its bell for thirty years, with the burial ground behind it. The druid school at Caol shean promises a yearly teacher for what congregation remains.

title: The first lecture at the empty quarter
summary: A young teacher of the druid school at Caol shean comes to Muileann dhearg in am Faoilleach and finds four old people and the caretaker Padraig Iarna waiting in the cold hall. He does not come again that year sooner than the next am Faoilleach.
